chapter: Ben Webster, Tatum and Los Angeles scene
title: Race: no problems then; opinion on violence
summary: He says there were no race problems in the early 1940s, voices views on Martin Luther King and violence, and says he preferred Black musicians.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: No, not then. None of that stuff those days. Not a bit. It wasn't until Martin Luther King came along with his "Four Hundred Years of Slavery" and "I Had A Dream" and all that... Well, I'm all for him. And I think everybody should

be equal -- everybody. But let's not just climb in everybody's window and, just because they happen to be White, beat the livin' daylights out of 'em and all that stuff, you know, and riot and all that. Let's just get along! I don't believe in all that violence. I don't care if a guy's Ethiopian, Arabic, Jewish, Polish, whatever the hell he is -- I don't care. As long as he's a good guy, he's a good guy -- period. Don't you think so?

Hell yes! I worked with so many Black guys that I didn't know what it was like... When I played with White guys, I felt out of place, hah-hah-hah-hah, because I was always playing with the Black guys or playing for a Black singer. And I didn't give a damn. I was happy.
